question: Which circulation route carries low-oxygen (deoxygenated) blood from the heart to the lungs?
explanation: You've got this! The pulmonary circulation is simply the pathway that sends deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart straight to the lungs to pick up fresh oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of the systemic circulation?

options.B: Cooling down the surface of the skin

explanation: Great job! Once the blood gets oxygen from the lungs, the systemic circulation pumps it out to feed all the organs and tissues throughout the rest of your body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which blood vessels act like control valves to help regulate blood pressure?
explanation: Spot on! Arterioles have smooth muscle walls that can tighten or relax. This changing size helps control resistance and keeps your blood pressure in check. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why do arteries need such thick, muscular walls?

options.A: To prevent the backflow of blood using valves
options.B: To absorb nutrients directly from passing blood
options.C: To store extra blood reserves for emergencies
options.D: To withstand high pressure from heart contractions

explanation: Think of arteries as receiving blood right as it leaves the powerhouse heart. Because the pressure is so high with every beat, they need strong, thick walls not to burst! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h2)

question: What makes capillary walls so good at passing substances back and forth?

options.B: Thick rings of smooth muscle tissue
options.C: An outer layer of tough fibrous cartilage
options.D: A single layer of endothelial cells

explanation: You're doing great! Capillaries are super thin—just one cell thick—which makes it really easy for oxygen and nutrients to slip right through to your tissues. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h3)

question: Where in the body does the actual exchange of oxygen and nutrients take place?
explanation: Exactly! Because capillary walls are so microscopically thin, they are the main trading posts where oxygen, waste, and nutrients move between the blood and body cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of valves inside human veins?

options.B: Preventing the backward flow of blood

explanation: Well done! Veins have a tough job fighting gravity to get blood back up to the heart. Their one-way valves make sure blood only moves forward and doesn't slide backward. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h4)

question: How do your skeletal muscles help blood move through your veins?

options.A: By relaxing to create a vacuum in capillaries
options.B: By squeezing the veins to push blood upward
options.C: By producing heat to thin the blood plasma
options.D: By pumping oxygen directly into the vessel walls

explanation: Think of your muscles as a natural pump! When you move and your skeletal muscles flex, they physically squeeze nearby veins, pushing the blood upward toward your heart. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which middle layer of a blood vessel wall is mostly made of smooth muscle?
explanation: You've got this! 'Media' means middle. The tunica media is the middle layer packed with smooth muscle and elastic fibers that lets vessels change size. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is the very inner lining of a blood vessel (tunica intima) kept so smooth?

options.A: To absorb oxygen directly from the lumen
options.B: To minimize friction against flowing blood
options.C: To allow rapid diffusion of white blood cells
options.D: To prevent the vessel walls from collapsing

explanation: Makes total sense, right? A smooth inner lining helps blood glide smoothly without getting stuck, preventing unwanted clots or turbulence. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which factor has the biggest and most immediate effect on blood flow resistance?

options.C: Total length of the body veins

explanation: Spot on! Even a tiny change in how wide or narrow a blood vessel is (its radius) makes a massive difference in how hard it is for blood to flow through. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the main driving force that pushes blood through the circulatory system?
explanation: You're doing great! Just like air rushing out of a balloon, blood naturally flows from areas of high pressure to areas of lower pressure. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the main underlying issue in atherosclerosis?

options.A: Clotting of blood inside heart chambers
options.B: Buildup of fatty plaques inside arteries
options.C: Weakening of venous valves in the legs
options.D: Dilation of capillaries in lung tissues

explanation: Keep it up! Atherosclerosis happens when fats and cholesterol build up inside the arteries, forming plaques that narrow the passage for blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h7)

question: What common problem happens when the valves in your leg veins stop working properly?

options.A: Pooling of blood and swelling in the legs
options.B: Rapid clotting within the pulmonary trunk
options.C: Extreme high pressure in systemic arterioles
options.D: Sudden plaque rupture inside coronary arteries

explanation: You nailed it! If vein valves get weak, they can't stop gravity from pulling the blood back down, causing it to pool up and lead to swollen, heavy legs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h7)
